items.body: It's rare to come back home empty-handed from a foray into Corbett vs Dempsey’s territorial waters, and this mission is no exception. Today, we're talking about the Atlantic Pact, set between the ever-erupting, volcanic Chicago scene and the anarcho-free stronghold of Amsterdam, that nothing and no one will ever conquer. No drones, tanks, Patriots, or F-35s, but the only weapons useful to humanity: reeds, pianos, drums, and basses. These Things Happen provide them with their sophomore album, "A Gentle Reminder", following their 2022 self-titled debut. This album, recorded at Hyde Park Jazz Festival in Chicago and at WNUR Studio, Northwestern University, confirms the band's recipe: original songs interspersed with renditions of Misha Mengelberg and Thelonious Monk, presented not in a slavish, calligraphic manner but through a contemporary reinterpretation of tradition. The players on the field deserve to be met up close. Keefe Jackson, tenor saxophone, bass clarinet. Born in Fayetteville, Arkansas, he arrived in Chicago in 2001 and performed across US and Europe with the likes of Tomeka Reid, Tim Days, Dave Rempis, Mike Reed, Jeb Bishop, Jason Adasiewicz, Satoko Fujii, Ab Baars and Bill Meyer. His partner in crime on the other side of the Pond, Oscar Jan Hoogland, piano, is a top notch badass. A leading figure on the Dutch impro scene, Hoogland sprung onto the Amsterdam landscape around 20 years ago, at the forefront of a new group of improvisers to arrive and simultaneously uphold the tradition of New Dutch Swing even while tearing it apart. As always, collaborations define the breadth of a musician's chromatic palette and so, read here about Oscar: improvisation with Senegalese singer Mola Sylla and percussionist Frank Rosaly; sound installations and performances with Practical Music and his Phonograph Orchestra; cumbia with Ibelisse Guardia Ferraguttis’s Superinca and the Galactic Green; Ethiopian jazz and Eritrean traditional music with Semer Welday’s Adulis. His work with Arnold de Boer and the duo with mythologic Han Bennink incontrovertibly attests to the caliber of the artist. The rhythm section that supports the two pals features Jason Roebke on double bass (collaborations with Ken Vandermark, Jeb Bishop, Jeff Parker, Chad Taylor, and Rob Mazurek), who replaced Joshua Abrams during the process, and Mikel Patrick Avery on drums (Rob Mazurek, Marshall Allen Tomeka Reid, Jeff Parker, and Kurt Vile on his CV). The record: Jackson's opening track "20 Years Past 12 O'Clock," a sonic excursus that moves across multiple time scales, is followed by a piece by Hoogland dedicated to Ab Baars, "Upperclass Underground," and a reinterpretation of Monk’s "Green Chimneys," whose genesis is described as follows: "it started out as a punk song on the setlist before taking a thin-threaded turn on the night." Two original compositions keep the pace in the right mood, constantly balancing compositional rigor with a loose flow, free from excessive constraints. The revisitation of Mengelberg's "Een Beetje Zenuwachtig," from minor to major, pays homage to the legendary Ukrainian pianist's key change when he played "Round Midnight" in Chicago, while "Well You Needn't" pushes Monk "max so far," as Hoogland puts it, with a sculptural declination of an ongoing sonic pendulum swinging between modernity and tradition. The album closes with “Over het Zijn en het Hoera”, its title drawn from an absurdist story by Dutch writer and artist Armando. As it has rightly been said, this is music that knows its history inside out and wears it lightly. The generosity of spirit here, between players, between cities, between Monk and Mengelberg, between composition and the moment, is the real subject. You know, sometimes things like these happen. items.body:
BURNOUT SYNDROMES are celebrating a decade since their major debut by returning to where it all began.

On 19 August, the Japanese rock trio released Haikyu!! BOS - Syudaikatachinoutage -, a special cover album dedicated to the beloved anime Haikyu!!. Translating to “Banquet of Theme Songs,” the record sees the band revisiting the music that has soundtracked the series through their own interpretations.

BURNOUT SYNDROMES' history with Haikyu!! stretches back to their 2016 major-label debut, when 'FLY HIGH!!' was selected as an opening theme for the anime's second season. They later returned with 'hikariare' and 'PHOENIX', further cementing the series as a defining part of the band's musical journey.

For their 10th anniversary, the Osaka trio have turned the spotlight on the wider Haikyu!! soundtrack. The 12-track album features their takes on songs originally performed by SPYAIR, NICO Touches the Walls, Sukima Switch, tacica, CHiCO with HoneyWorks, and SUPER BEAVER, alongside BURNOUT SYNDROMES' own Haikyu!! themes.

The album artwork also features specially drawn illustrations from Haikyu!!, bringing the worlds of the band and the anime together once more. Coinciding with the release, a JUMP MV for 'PHOENIX' featuring illustrations from Haruichi Furudate's Haikyu!! manga premiered today.

BURNOUT SYNDROMES are also headed to the Philippines next month. The band will perform at BURNOUT SYNDROMES LIVE IN MANILA 2026 on 5 September at The Crossroad Center, with the show scheduled to begin at 6 PM. Get tickets here.

items.body:
Japanese singer-songwriter Centimillimental has joined forces with Indonesian singer-songwriter Arash Buana for 'madoromi', an intimate ballad born from a chance studio session.

Released on 19 August, the track marks Centimillimental's first-ever collaboration release and arrives alongside a music video filmed during the pair's recording sessions in Indonesia.

Written and composed by both artists, 'madoromi' captures the hazy space between sleep and wakefulness, tracing feelings that surface in the quiet of the night. Their voices meet over a dreamy soundscape, reflecting the natural chemistry that first brought the song together.

The collaboration began after Centimillimental met Buana during his Asia tour in 2025. What started without plans to make or release a song quickly developed into 'madoromi.'

"When we met, talked about various things, and I listened to some of his songs, I felt that we shared similar ideas and certain commonalities in our musical sensibilities," Centimillimental shared.

"As we continued our studio sessions, occasionally talking along the way, before we knew it, we had created a song. That song was 'madoromi.'"

For Buana, that connection was almost immediate. The Indonesian artist revealed that the track's main melody and foundation came together within the first 15 to 30 minutes of their session.

"We weren't overthinking things or trying to force the song into a particular shape. We simply decided to let things unfold naturally," he said.

Despite not sharing the same first language, the two found common ground in the studio. "It reminded me once again that there are moments when you can communicate even when you don't speak the same language," Buana added. "I feel that the music itself became our language."

Fans in Jakarta received an early taste of the collaboration in July, when Buana made a surprise appearance at Centimillimental's show in the Indonesian capital for the pair's first-ever live performance of 'madoromi.'

The song's accompanying music video brings listeners even closer to its beginnings, featuring footage of Centimillimental and Buana creating and recording the track together in Indonesia.

For his first collaboration release, Centimillimental hopes 'madoromi' finds listeners in exactly the kind of quiet moment that inspired it.

"I hope you'll listen to this song while drifting into that hazy state before falling asleep, thinking of someone important to you," he shared.

items.body:
For record collectors, half the fun is never knowing what you are going to find.

That spirit of discovery sits at the heart of Lifted Trax, a new specialist record store at 25 Lorong Telok, in the middle of Singapore's music and nightlife district. From secondhand dance records and rare groove to new releases from artists and labels across Asia, the shop is designed as somewhere listeners can dig deep, discover something unfamiliar, and stay awhile.

Tucked away on the third floor of a shophouse, Lifted Trax is the project of Singapore-based DJ, producer, and label head Jordan Glick, who performs and releases music as Dexter Colt and runs the labels Darker Than Wax and Super Enjoy.

Canadian-born Glick has lived in Singapore for 20 years, and left a corporate career in the music industry to build the record store. While the idea had been on his mind for some time, a trip to Japan in May 2025 ultimately pushed him to make it happen.

“The idea had been kicking around in my head for a while,” Glick shared. “Then I was in Japan for some gigs, and all my free time between shows was spent digging — Revelation Time, Rare Groove and Compufunk in Osaka, Mole Music in Nara, Rana Musica and Ella Records in Tokyo.”

It wasn't only the records that stayed with him.

“Something about talking to the owners and spending hours in those rooms made me realise record shops are my favourite spaces in the world — and some of the most important spaces for community building in local music scenes,” he continued. “I came home extremely inspired and started working on Lifted Trax straight away.”

A shop made for the long dig

That Japanese record-store experience helped shape what Lifted Trax would eventually become.

Its secondhand collection moves across dance and electronic music, ambient and new age, reggae and dancehall, jazz, soul, disco, rare groove, and other sounds, with the emphasis firmly on a tightly selected catalogue rather than simply filling as many crates as possible.

Alongside those secondhand records is a smaller new-release section with a strong focus on artists and labels from across Asia. Independent dance music from North America and Europe also makes its way onto the shelves, including records that previously may have required Singapore listeners to order internationally or pick up while travelling.

The result is a selection that draws inspiration from specialist shops in Japan, New York, and London while placing music from Asia prominently within the mix.

There is more than vinyl to browse, too. Lifted Trax stocks vinyl care products, turntable accessories, incense, zines, and other goods for anyone looking to spend considerably more time around a record player.

For Glick, though, what happens to a record after it leaves the shop can be just as interesting as how it arrived there.

Some of Lifted Trax's secondhand stock comes from older DJs in Singapore, allowing records that once soundtracked the city's dancefloors to find their way into the collections of another generation.

“I get most excited when records sourced from an older DJ’s collection get picked up by a younger DJ,” he said.

“This physical object that was moving dancefloors in Singapore twenty, thirty years ago is getting a new life, and will continue to be part of the city’s dance music culture. That perpetuation of musical heritage, in such a tangible way, is one of the main reasons I love records.”

It is a particularly fitting cycle for a store built around secondhand music: one DJ lets go of a record, another finds it years later, and the same piece of wax enters a different chapter of Singapore's club culture.

From Lorong Telok to the rest of Asia

Lifted Trax may have a physical home in Singapore, but Glick is also looking beyond the city.

The store ships its entire collection — both secondhand records and new releases — throughout Asia. That means listeners and collectors in places such as Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, and Hong Kong can shop from the same catalogue as someone dropping by the store in person.

It also gives Lifted Trax a wider role within a region where specialist records can often be spread across different cities and scenes.

While the shelves are naturally a major part of the experience, Glick's ambitions for the shop go beyond retail.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lifted Trax Record Store (@liftedtrax)

Lifted Trax is expected to host in-store events, organise club nights around Singapore, and eventually operate in-house record labels, extending the project into a broader platform for the musicians, DJs, listeners, and communities around it.

“I hope the shop contributes to the growing landscape of cultural spaces here,” Glick shared, “by being a place to meet like-minded people, exchange ideas, and forge musical connections in the local scene.”

And what exactly should an afternoon there feel like?

For Glick, the answer does not involve anything overly complicated.

“Buzzing but calm, nice light coming through the windows, and a great track you’ve never heard before coming through the speakers.”

For anyone who has ever lost an afternoon flicking through crates, that probably says enough.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lifted Trax Record Store (@liftedtrax)

Lifted Trax is located at 25 Lorong Telok #03-01, Singapore 049037. The store is open from 12 PM to 7 PM on Wednesdays and Thursdays, 12 PM to 8 PM on Fridays and Saturdays, and 12 PM to 6 PM on Sundays, and is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.

Lifted Trax also ships its secondhand and new-release collections throughout Asia. For more information, visit www.liftedtrax.com, follow @liftedtrax on Instagram, or contact +65 8083 3184 / contact@liftedtrax.com

items.body:
Alexandra Hainsworth has taken former New Zealand record label Do It Management and music distributor The Orchard to court, alleging copyright and contract breaches as well as unpaid royalties.

The British-Australian pop singer filed the case through her company, Inspire Create Pty Ltd, in the High Court at Auckland. The Orchard is a subsidiary of Sony Music Entertainment.

According to documents seen by Stuff, Hainsworth entered into an agreement with Do It Management in March 2022 for the promotion, publishing, and distribution of her music in New Zealand. Under the agreement, she was reportedly entitled to 50% of profits after expenses.

Hainsworth alleged that Do It Management failed to properly track and pay her royalties. Do It Management reportedly disputes the claims.

The dispute escalated in late 2024, with Hainsworth later seeking to terminate the agreement. She also claimed that her catalogue was removed from Spotify without her permission after legal proceedings began.

The singer’s most-streamed track, 'Fighter', has accumulated more than 1.4 million Spotify streams. Her manager Victor Paul said she has released 27 tracks to date.

Hainsworth told Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand that the legal dispute has also prevented her from releasing new music, including two tracks made with Brazilian producer VINNE.

“I’ve got two tracks that were supposed to be out like a year ago,” she said. “These are excellent tracks that need to be going out there in the world, but I haven’t been able to do it.”

Hainsworth said the case has since reached a memorandum stage before a judge in the High Court.

Asked what she hopes to get out of the proceedings, she told Rolling Stone: “Just being able to be a normal musician again.”

Unmixed later reported that Hainsworth’s proceedings specifically name The Orchard Enterprises NY, Inc., and alleged that royalties have been withheld while new releases have remained blocked for more than 20 months.

The Orchard declined to comment to Unmixed, while a lawyer understood by Stuff to be acting for the company said he was “not interested in commenting”.

The case remains before the High Court at Auckland.

items.body:
Iman Fandi has taken her music to Los Angeles.

The Singaporean singer-songwriter performed at Snoop Dogg's Compound in Los Angeles on 15 August for Superstar Among Friends: Broadus Together, an invitation-only TikTok LIVE event featuring Snoop Dogg. The livestream garnered 76 million in total exposure.

Held at Snoop Dogg's private 20,000-square-foot creative campus, the event was co-produced by Gushcloud International alongside Cordell Broadus, Death Row Games, and CMC Shine SEA, and hosted by Boss Lady Entertainment as part of TikTok LIVE Fest 2026.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Iman Fandi Ahmad (@imanfandi17)

Fandi marked the occasion with the international debut of her forthcoming single, 'It Is', which is slated for release on 21 August.

The performance came on the heels of a busy run for the Gushcloud artist, which included taking part in Singapore's National Day celebrations and performing at the Istana.

“Being part of NDP 2026 was already such a huge milestone for me,” shared Fandi. Reflecting on her trip to Los Angeles, she added: “LA, especially, felt like more than just another performance, it felt like a door opening to something bigger.”

The night also saw Snoop Dogg take to the decks as DJ Snoopadelic, with his set featuring 'Drop It Like It's Hot'. The lineup included Filipino-Australian singer and actress Ylona Garcia, Lady of Rage, Jane Handcock, Charlie Bereal, Kalvin Love, and Princess Broadus, who closed the event with a DJ set.

Viewers tuning in online were also given a look inside the Broadus family's Compound through a tour led by Snoop Dogg's son, Cordell Broadus. The tour took audiences through spaces including recording studios, a games room, and a basketball court.

“For me, this is all about ownership and bringing our culture to new spaces,” said Broadus, co-founder of Death Row Games. He added that bringing together the Death Row family, artists, and creators at the Compound — alongside TikTok, Gushcloud, and CMC Shine — helped put the event “in front of a global audience”.

Behind the scenes, Singaporean creatives also played a key role in bringing the show to life. Creative director Melissa Sim, founder and co-artistic director of Singapore theatre company How Drama, led the show's overall creative vision and worked on its scripting and TikTok audience engagement.

The Singapore team also included livestream director Sheng Hong Lo of Poco Productions, production manager Ross Nasir of How Drama, and show caller Rosie Putri of How Drama.

“It was an international affair and I'm glad we got to represent Singapore on the global stage,” said Sim.

items.body:
Slowspin Combines Ambient-Jazz & Hindustani Folk On New Album 'AFTERIMAGE'

19 August 2026

'Afteimage', the latest album by Zeekar Ahmed aka SLOWSPIN, isn't the first time the U.S.-based Karachi-rooted artist has expressed the inner worlds of the diaspora. Her archival sound installation 'Mother, I Am Compelled to Leave' has done that before. Neither is it the first time she has combined folk influences with contemporary instrumentation. That's been done with similar themes on her previous critically lauded album 'TALISMAN'.

However, the new 10-track record sees her grip the universality in both aspects tighter and shed off the excess further with a minimalist approach. The blunt, heavy hits of drums with brushes or mallets, clean guitar strums, and sometimes harps and woodwinds too, put the work in the textural jazz palette along with its slightly improvisational nature. The simple melodies on tracks like lullaby-like 'Jaat Rahi' or the sustained longings of 'Hari Hari' add a safe consonance to the album, while a track like 'Mausam / Broken Hearted One' layers its melodies till its shapes obscure into a bed. All of these instances give 'TALISMAN' an ambient effect but with a dynamic character, creating a standout lexicon for the album that is truly its crown jewel.

Meanwhile, the influence of the folk canon, no doubt informed by Ahmed's academic and curatorial work on South Asian female folk musical traditions, opens up the themes of the album from just the diaspora experience to anyone who has had to move away from loved ones, said emotional goodbyes, felt the need for them and longed for the life before them at the same time.

The English-language songwriting on the album does add variation to the album, but they don't share the perfect marriage with the placating soft instrumentation and the focused sentimentality of the patient melodic expression on a single word that the Braj, Hindustani and Urdu counterparts feature. It's the latter world where 'AFTERIMAGE' functions best, creating a sonic world where it can take flight into shoegazy crescendos like on 'Mother I Have To Leave' or stay convinced in a memorable, delicate performance as in 'Jaat Rahi'.

Listen to 'Afterimage' below and follow Slowspin for more information.

items.body: With first quarter of 21st century, Iranian sound artist Pé continues a trajectory that began with gold bars made in dubai (2025) and gathered momentum on 40.8 tonnes of freedom (2025), moving away from the metaphysical concerns of earlier releases towards an engagement with what he describes as “shrugged off crimes against humanity.” However, the shift is not as abrupt as it first appears. If albums such as æzæl: eternity of nonexistence (2025), æbæd: through imagining eternity (2024), and æm: representations of nonexistence (2024) used abstract synthesiser improvisations to examine nonexistence and cosmological time, the recent works retain the same compositional discipline while redirecting it towards contemporary history. For Pé, this is not a rupture but an evolution: an attempt to extend philosophical enquiry through what he calls a “transdisciplinary approach.” That continuity is immediately apparent in the music itself. The four compositions remain resolutely abstract, built from slowly evolving drones, unstable resonances, distortion and spectral interference rather than melody or rhythm. Despite titles such as “82,448 palestinians,” “conservatively confirmed death toll,” and “courtesy of state of israel,” there are no documentary recordings, no explicit musical illustrations of violence, and no attempt to dictate an emotional response. Instead, the gulf between the factual precision of the titles and the ambiguity of the sound becomes the album’s central compositional device. As Pé suggests, that space is deliberately left for the listener to confront through their own cultural, political and personal position. Compared to 40.8 tonnes of freedom (2025), first quarter of 21st century feels noticeably tighter and more compressed. The earlier EP allowed individual spectral layers greater autonomy, often opening vast acoustic spaces in which metallic resonances, drones and noise could coexist with remarkable transparency. Here the pressure rarely lifts. Each piece explores a different manifestation of instability: the slowly mutating density of the title track, the relentless fragmentation of “82,448 palestinians,” the devastating restraint of “conservatively confirmed death toll,” and the architectural synthesis of “courtesy of state of israel.” Throughout, Pé continues to compose almost exclusively through the redistribution of spectral energy, microscopic timbral shifts and long-form transformations, demonstrating an exceptional command of electroacoustic form. The accompanying Bandcamp warning — “Listener discretion advised. Extreme frequencies low and high moderate volume suggested to avoid possible damages, please be cautious psychoacoustic effects intended” — proves more than justified. Pé’s music has always been deeply concerned with the physical experience of listening, and the sub-bass pressure, abrasive upper frequencies and carefully controlled beating phenomena are integral to the compositions. Those self-imposed limitations, including the recurring use of the ARP Odyssey and minimal post-production, have become a deliberately restricted vocabulary through which different conceptual territories can be explored. Few contemporary electroacoustic releases negotiate the relationship between abstraction and political reality with such confidence. Rather than attempting to sonically represent conflict, first quarter of 21st century insists that the listener complete the work themselves. In doing so, it transforms listening into an ethical act, where sound becomes not an illustration of history but a space in which our relationship to it is quietly, and uncompromisingly, tested. To better understand his production process we reached out directly to Pé who kindly agreed to answer four questions over an email exchange. Your earlier releases—ædæm: representations of nonexistence, æbæd: through imagining eternity, and æzæl: eternity of nonexistence—were concerned with philosophical questions of time, existence, and cosmology, often expressed through abstract titles and long-form synthesizer improvisations. Beginning with gold bars made in dubai, which confronted the war in Sudan through the global trade in gold, and continuing with 40.8 tonnes of freedom and now first quarter of 21st century, your work has become increasingly explicit in its engagement with contemporary conflicts and political violence. What prompted this shift? Do you see these recent releases as a rupture with your earlier work, or do they emerge from the same philosophical concerns viewed through the realities of the present? To start with what has prompted the shift from philosophical topics to contemporary conflicts; it was an attempt to moving towards “transdisciplinary approach” and progressing from – so called – philosophical thought experiments, by borrowing from journalism. therefore i am a bit reluctant to view these projects as a rupture from past practices rather than some form of evolution, since they are still a call for attention to “ignorance”. The titles of first quarter of 21st century—”82,448 palestinians”, “conservatively confirmed death toll”, and “courtesy of state of israel”—leave no room for ambiguity. Yet the music itself remains instrumental, refusing illustration or overt emotional cues. What relationship were you hoping to establish between these stark factual titles and the abstract electronic sound world? Did you want listeners to experience the tension between documentation and interpretation rather than being directed toward a single emotional response? The refusal of illustration and a directed emotional response, as you mentioned, is the manner which I appreciate most in art, regardless of form/field; for its insistence on self reflection that the audience should bear. Trying to sonically represent (in the tone discussed) what the title says, or to be more precise the gap between them, would be filled by the audience confronting their stance, personally or culturally, on the subject. Across your discography there is a striking consistency in your working methods: extreme frequencies, minimal editing, the recurring use of the ARP Odyssey, and an emphasis on limitation as a compositional principle. Even as the conceptual focus has shifted from metaphysics to contemporary history, your sonic language has remained remarkably coherent. What continues to attract you to these self-imposed constraints? Do they allow you to respond to radically different subjects without changing your musical vocabulary? The self-imposed constraints are mostly for avoiding redundancy as well as driving creativity. Of course the personal preferences of frequency ranges, prepared signal chains and doing the least in DAW, are still shaping much of the sonic characteristics. Although, the limitations of choosing ARP Odyssey module as the sole source might be too many, its availability is what makes it convenient enough for now. Combining all these has given me access to some sort of primal sonic vocabulary (in my opinion) which leaves plenty room for expression in the manner discussed before, regardless of topic. You are an Iranian artist releasing music at a moment when questions of war, state violence, displacement, and historical memory don’t just affect you personally but resonate across the region. gold bars made in dubai, 40.8 tonnes of freedom, and first quarter of 21st century all engage with different conflicts while avoiding overt musical illustration. Do you think artists have a responsibility to bear witness to political reality, or is your work simply a personal response to living through the first quarter of the twenty-first century? Subjects of the releases you mentioned can be described as “shrugged off crimes against humanity”, and the responsibility of paying attention to these – and the normalized ignorance towards them – does not fall upon a certain group; bearing or avoiding these responsibilities can be rooted in different aspects of one’s identity and principles, as well as their dedication to cling to the bubble they live in. In short, the answer to this question is both, responsibility as an artist, and personal response as a witness. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: The Cardboard Falcon is a profoundly vibrant, impressionistic, cinematic, slow-moving, and melodically oriented neoclassical album that will lead the listener to a state of serenity and contemplation. Shrouded by a sense of elegance and touching grace the cardboard falcon by mico nonet   Mico Nonet is a multi-faceted and semiclassical ambient chamber orchestra from Santa Barbara (California). The line-up is a quintet with Efe Baltacigil on cello, Carrie Dennis on viola, Katherine Needleman on oboe, oboe d’amore, English horn, David Cooper on French horn, and Joshua Lee Kramer on synthesizer, guitar. All musicians are skilled and have integrated valuable positions in various orchestras such as Baltimore Symphony Orchestra, Philadelphia Orchestra… I must say that the musical background is quite impressive, meaningful, and solid. Joshua Lee Kramer is the sound artist who subtly articulates the various acoustic musical components through imaginative electronic filters and treatments. I used to love the innovative and brilliant musical dialogues between acoustic instrumentation and electronic devices such as Murcof, Hauschka, Michael Jacaszek in their respective works. Contrary to a critically acclaimed project such as Kiasmos, the electronic ingredients are reduced to the minimum to give major space to expressive acoustic and neoclassical instrumentation. You will not find heavy beat-laden atmospheres here but more emotionally transportive, soothing, enveloping, and vibrant cinematic sequences, shrouded by a sense of elegance and touching grace, sublimated by meandering electronic textures and discreet oscillations. The album succeeds in creating a deep interaction between warm, breathing organic phrases and more disembodied abstract motifs. All tracks flow harmoniously, guided by a sense of melodious sorrow and deliciously enriched by slight presences of hope rising at a distance. All in all, The Cardboard Falcon is a profoundly vibrant, impressionistic, cinematic, slow-moving, and melodically oriented neoclassical album that will lead the listener to a state of serenity and contemplation. Recommended listening experience for introspective healing moments and lonesome days. Fans of neoromantic music with electro-acoustic arrangements like Högni (Erased Tapes) or Icelandic composers for Bedroom Community won’t be disconcerted. The Cardboard Falcon is available on Ninevolt Labs. [Bandcamp] the cardboard falcon by mico nonetThe post mico nonet :: The Cardboard Falcon (Ninevolt Labs) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by maxsmusic — When this live album was released, I was a teenager living in Danbury Connecticut. I was in Junior High School and my friends turned me on to Gentle Giant. I was a struggling guitar player trying to learn the pentatonic scale and relate it to blues. Gentle Giant was another world. This was not pentatonics, this was extreme jazz with rock sensibilities. It's like the classically trained keyboardist took the band into the land of esoteric rock music. The vocals are very complex and they have multiple layers. Gentle Giant went into territory no other band would dare to explore. This was extreme esoteric music and it hit me hard as a teenager in 1975. I decided to become a musician due to this band. I now play classical guitar. Gentle Giant is like a rose in the garden of weeds. I love all their albums, even the late stuff that is more commercial. Giant for a Day was the low water mark but they recovered with Civilian and that album is brooding and very good. I would have loved to have seen the Giant when they toured the US in the mid seventies but I was a stupid kid with no money. The first concert I went to was Kiss in 1977. Gentle Giant is like fine wine that is worth $200 a bottle. You will never drink it because it is too valuable but you will stare at the label and think of its beauty in your imagination. The imagination is everything as Wallace Stevens told us.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — This Japanese quintet is quite distinctive: first, they use the sitar, an instrument that clearly shapes their sound and compositions; second, they feature two guitars; and third, the vocals are handled by their drummer, Go Kurosawa, who also founded the independent label Guruguru Brain.Following the "Semicircle" intro, which could easily belong to a 1970s band, "Kodama" shifts into the present day with an indie-alternative vibe and a blues foundation, gradually easing into a psychedelic atmosphere; layers of guitar and bass overlap and intertwine seamlessly, creating an impenetrable texture, like a net that catches us and holds us fast.On "Smoke and Mirrors," one of the guitars sounds like an organ, and then they launch into a psychedelic funk-rock jam where Jimi Hendrix intertwines with Dave Brubeck; they sound raw, and Go Kurosawa's vocals are as unpolished as Damo Suzuki's in Can, a deliberate effect, that roughness which wasn't there before but, upon arriving, imbued the music with a different hue, knowing just when to pause and stop to watch the paintings on the walls come to life and move... vibrating as if there were a 3D effect."Streets of Calcutta" features a bass-driven sound, bordering on stoner rock, over which the sitar begins to improvise; this fusion of eras and genres reminded me of The Move's album Looking On, where Roy Wood was at his creative best. The use of polyrhythms is evident, and it is not without reason that the style is likened to the more daring Krautrock of the 1970s."Hem" begins in a distinctly progressive style, offering an exciting journey driven by the lead guitar and backed by the rhythm guitar within a dense, dramatic atmosphere; its complex structure constantly shifts rhythms while accelerating relentlessly toward the finale. It is raw, unadulterated, and dense psychedelia.The tribal atmosphere hinted at throughout the album fully erupts at the end; "White Moon" feels like venturing into the forest to hear crickets and cuckoos. If the childlike drawing on the cover seems to darken, it is not merely an optical illusion created by the music, but the actual onset of nightfall?meanwhile, the sitar, played by Ryu Kurosawa, the drummer and bandleader's brother (who learned the instrument in Calcutta under musician Manilal Nag, inspiring the song "Streets of Calcutta") accompanies Ryu's vocals.Like a mantra, he repeats the final notes that bring down the curtain on yet another performance where East and West become one.

items.body: Review by maxsmusic — The new version, ca., 2026 is a big improvement over the original. Everything is now bright, in your face and crisp. The original mix was a bit muddy and even the band thought it needed to be remixed. So it only took 53 years but here we are. I think this album is peak Giant. They were writing material that was esoteric but extremely percussive. Kerry sings on more tracks than previous albums and he has a fragile voice that is emotive. This may be the most uncommercial Gentle Giant Album in their catalogue and it had to be imported into the USA in 1973. I have the import released by WWA Records. The new remix is Alucard, which is the Gentle Giant label. I have to give this album 5+ stars. It is actually 6 stars. No other band came close to Gentle Giant in their ambition, creativity, execution and emotion. They are the cream of the crop and no other band will play at this level. This is the highest form of art in music.

items.body: Review by Nickmannion — There is a relevance in my intro here...as back in the day in Manchester there used to be a record warehouse called initially Yanks, then Power Cut. I discovered it in the late 70s and it was there till the mid to late 90s. Their main source of stock, which I assume they bought by the pallet load for cents per ten, were cut outs and returns from the States. And they used to knock it out at 99p/�1.29/�1.49/�1.99 an album so you could go in with your �20 (I know, I know...) and come home with 12 albums. It was still the best way to discover new bands or fill gaps in your (at that period my fledgling) collection...Come Taste The Band by Deep Purple for instance (I played it last night, the US release copy I bought there) being my spring to mind example. Yes you may have come home with a couple of clunkers but it also massively broadened your horizons....a Mahavishnu Orchestra release and a Return To Forever album blowing my tiny mind and turning me on to jazz/rock/fusion which I may never have gone near in a million years. So yup, the Pentwater album* looked interesting enough and was �1.29 very well spent 45 years ago. I confess it took a little getting to know as I guess a Montrose/Aerosmith vibe might have been the instant appeal I wanted back then but it was worth hanging on to. Then, and even now, I would have called it 'Art Rock' especially as the intro track Frustration Mass struck me as Zappa (yup about 10 albums over the years from Power Cut!) in a really bad mood or maybe Henry Cow after supplements had worn off. Intriguing if not headbanging....unless you count 'against the wall'. I can now retro fit my expanded knowledge and say a dirtier version of Happy The Man too. There's even a psych type bridge section that adds interest and shows a breadth of influences. Track 2 (Living Room Displays) has a more recognisable keyboard led 'prog' groove that , again with retro knowledge, suggests several bands and a pinch of Kraut maybe. Memo is a more familiar guitar arpeggio song, if not quite mainstream rock then at least less left field. Orphan Girl begins with a Crimson melancholia before several prog bases are firmly touched but in a 'natural' rather than forced construct. AM has strong overtones of say the first two Be Bop Deluxe albums, Palendrobe suggests a Gentle Genesis 'mash up' and War opens with very Atomic Rooster sounding keys with a generous layer of Quatermass sprinkled over. Gwens Madrigal is closer to Kansas do hard rock.I always qualify my use of comparisons being not meant to suggest a very derivative dogs breakfast but as a reference point for new to the band readers and hopefully listeners. Am the first to stick the boot in to slavish copyist bands (hello there Druid and Starcastle....yes....you) but Pentwater, especially from the time and place they came from, did absorb 'unfashionable' influences and turned them into something interesting and unexpected in parts. I now have the follow up album but don't rate it quite as high as the debut. The usual caveat, a 3.8+ rounded up to a 4. Enjoy. * My copy has the same track listing but in a different order to that listed here and, on a quick check, on Discogs too.

items.body: Review by ianjferris@gmail.com — I've seen all the reviews here of "Open Your Eyes" and believe me, I do understand why so many are scoring this album with only one or two stars, with some scathing commentary as an accompaniment. However, I can't do scathing for this album. It's too good for that. The musicians on it are much too good for that. I have to award this album four stars. When I look at this album with both my ears and my eyes open (all puns intended), the absence of Rick Wakeman is clearly obvious; but not in a negative way. I hear a very good album of pop songs (albeit with many being a bit on the quirkey side), put together by a collection of very experienced, very talented musicians. This isn't a progressive rock album. I don't believe that it was ever supposed to be a prog album. I think that at this stage, just after the "Keys To Ascension" recordings, the YES guys just might have been "all progged out". After all, they were all human (some still are, allegedly). The result was that all they had left was to put together some simple easy listening pop music pieces. Well, that's what it sounds like to me. The thing is though, said "simple easy listening pop music pieces" were actually being produced by serious prog rock musicians. And as a consequence, there are many musical flourishes evident throughout. And that's why it falls between two stools; two very distinct stools - good pop music and good prog music. There clearly are elements of both pop and prog here in this album. Just not enough to satisfy the purists (whether pop purists or prog purists). But outside of that, there is plenty to satisfy the broader mind. The only issue resides in the final, hidden (so called) track. Even for the most hardened, card carrying, prog adventurists, this one is a bit of a mystery. Mind you though, I can clearly imagine Squire, Anderson et al, smirking and sniggering mischievously at including this one curiosity.Anyway, I like this album enough to award it four stars.PS - I have the album on vinyl. Double album coloured vinyl. LP one is orange. LP two is red, both 180gram vinyl. It's one of 3000 copies that were issued by EAR Music.Just showing off.....

When I listened to it I didn't recognize some of the tunes. I went on the web and I read a comment that there had been a mix-up and the A-side was pressed with an unknown german band for some records.I let the thing drop and it was not until I started entering my record collection into Discogs that I picked up this thread a couple of years ago. I entered some of the phrases from the music on the strange A-side in websearch and out popped the A-side from the LP "The Groundhogs - Who Will Save The World? The Mighty Groundhogs" by the Groundhogs.So the root cause is a mixup by the recording company when the album was pressed. Mixing up the A-side for the records UAS 29237 vs UAS 29327.So I'm rating the faulty A-side 4 stars and the original B-side 3 stars.

items.body: Review by Nickmannion — I can't quite understand those who seem to want 50 year old recordings, probably never intended for release, to be 2026 audio perfection. Could you imagine how 'rock music' would have moved forward if those early 60's musicians had gone 'yeah that Robert Johnson might be ok but the sound quality of the recordings man...nah, couldn't get in to him'...and that only a 30 year hiatus. Digression...maybe...a point re archive recordings ... you betcha!Nektar seem to be good at polarising opinion too. There is definitely a camp who prefer their concept based structured and layered sound/albums and those (both hands in the air me) who can't get enough of the extended guitar fest jams, although I actually appreciate their other approach too. Funnily enough read reviews of the Sounds Like This album, which this tour was no doubt promoting, to see what I mean! So live Nektar was and is probably going to be of the latter approach as the more of their live stuff that appears, that seems to be front and centre of the eye so to speak.I tell you what...and we shouldn't always think of the guitar as the instrument to drool over...but the more I hear Roye Allbrighton, the more impressed I am and the more under-rated he was. But we have to admit they balanced this out on the two sets in question with 1234 and Preacher and add ons being the guitar heroics yet we get a sublime 20min plus version of Journey with all its more conventional prog twists and turns and the much welcomed 'concept'. I have to admit, when I first heard Nektar way way back in the day, I did think they were a German band and was well impressed with the lyrics and vocals for a second language! I am assuming I took that from hearing they were much more of a draw in mainland Europe, and had a foothold in the States too, yet a Sunday afternoon at The Roundhouse was probably their natural habitat in the UK, maybe even the college circuit. But this 2 disc set is a welcomed treasure and may re-calibrate those views on Sounds Like This. For information, on an open mind to music, there is a well known picture on an early Joy Division pic sleeve single or EP with a young Ian Curtis wearing a Nektar t-shirt. Some would say that is kudos, others that there is a lesson somewhere! Try this album and these recordings and appreciate an excellent band....both facets of....and not far from their peak. Yes a decimal point under 4 but you know...rounding up and all that.

items.body: Though the author’s scope ranges from the early 19th century to the present day, it is not a comprehensive history, rather it is a sort of micro history of a musical genre born of sadness, hate, anger, and political dominance. It is a genre I have chosen to call “classical protest music”. And, for the sake of this review, I am referring to the incorporation of protest as a valid and effective modality for the contemporary composer.of so called “western art music”, Until the very late 19th century, music served mostly entertainment, celebration, worship, and memorial functions. But this is about a new, if frequently discomforting voice for this art form. Music, like drama, and sometimes poetry are art forms that burn most brightly in performance. They exist on a page or even simply within the artist’s mind but come fully alive only in the temporal realm of performance. They then come to exist in the memories of the individuals who experience it. And those memories also exist concurrently within the overall social reality. Politics, philosophy, economics, and spirituality which ultimately frame art are now incorporated into the art form as it talks back to history. The function of protest music in the popular or vernacular genre, one that arguably has had a greater impact in fomenting political change than protest music in the guise of the western classical tradition, has been well documented. Not so with music of the concert hall classical format. Jeremy Eichler’s beautifully researched and written micro history makes a case for this art form framing (or reframing) history. Of course, not all expressions of protest hit the target of actually influencing history, but this book is not about that. It is about the birth of a concept little known in music until the late 19th and early 20th century. It is a genre which persists today in the so called political classical genre. The book is filled with historical facts and people which become metaphors as the author elucidates the historical contexts that, in retrospect, can be seen as the genesis of art not just passively responding to historical events. They are attempts to use art to comment about and, hopefully influence history and to express outrage, sadness, and to call for change. Music, ever the realm of entertainment and celebration, now increasingly finds purpose and mechanism to participate, not only as a supplier of entertainment and homage, but also as “a voice crying in the wilderness” in dialogue with the social/political milieu. Eichler chooses four musical pieces by four different composers from four different time periods to tell the story of the evolution of western art music to speak with in an informed, publicly intellectual voice. In its ideal presentation, it succeeds best when it resonates with the hearts and minds of the audience. That can and sometimes does “go viral” (in common parlance) and subsequently influences public opinion. The musical exemplars the author chooses includes: Richard Strauss (1864-1949) “Metamorphosen” (1946) Arnold Schoenberg (1874-1951) “A Survivor from Warsaw” (1947) Benjamin Britten (1913-1976) “War Requiem”(1962) Dimitri Shostakovich (1906-1975) “Symphony No. 13 ‘Babi Yar’” (1962) Each composer, each work is subjected to historical, philosophical, and (I would say) spiritual/mystical analysis. And, to accomplish this, he goes back first to the early 19th century to discuss the rise of the idealized German gconcept of “Bildung” and the subsequent rise of antisemitism famously touted as a necessary fact by Richard Wagner (1813-1883) and subsequently amplified to the extreme of The Shoah. Many musical works are referenced here, but John Foulds “A World Requiem” (1923), which is a large grandiose work of post romantic grandeur that seems to embody many of the elements that have come to characterize classical protest music. The work, written for large forces incorporates both liturgical and non-liturgical texts from disparate sources (not just western literature). It was conceived seemingly as a sort of final statement, a “requiem to end all requiems”, so to speak. Though popular in its day, it no more succeeded in preventing violence and hatred than Alexander Scriabin (1872-1915) in his unfinished Mysterium” succeeded in making the composer an immortal in a transcendent realm described from the spiritual imagination of Theosophical writings. But it did make a huge impact on protest as a valid modality for the artist. Protest in any modality doesn’t always have the intended impact. The point is the statement itself. Foulds’ work can be seen as a sort of precursor, if not template for Britten’s “War Requiem”. More importantly the success of Foulds’work revealed a sympathetic audience who doubtless saw in it a clarion call, a grandly hopeful expression to an audience hungry to resolve the hatred, anger, and sadness of the increasingly divided and chaotic world as it evolved post 1919. It spoke to a fervent hope for healing and transcendence and remains a historically significant work of musical art. Doubtless, many composers were delighted to identify this burgeoning need. Countless works followed Foulds’ noble effort and continue to this day in larger and smaller forces. Protest music, visual art, poetry, and drama are born of pain, sorrow, and hope derived from a sometimes pleading, sometimes shouting optimism. Much like audience engagement in sing alongs, audiences are invited to participate politically, emotionally and share the pain, sadness, and outrage as art speaks back to society rather than simply decorating it or celebrating it. Now, art embraces critique, not simply memorial. Eichler discusses each composer and work, contextualizing them historically, geographically, emotionally, and philosophically/spiritually. Richard Strauss He begins then, with Richard Strauss (1864-1949) and the only work cited here that does not have a vocal component or a text. It is also more a personal reaction rather than an a work explicitly engaging with politics and history. It remains the most unique and enigmatic piece in the oeuvre of a man who remained, if not always happily, employed from the late nineteenth century, through two world wars and horrific historical events and wildly differing leaders. To this listener’s ears, it seems more of a catharsis, a musical processing of the composer’s emotions and possibly exorcizing them and containing them in this music. It is truly a powerful piece but it does not rise to the more explicit protest works that would follow in the mid twentieth century. Arnold Schoenberg A very convincing and insightful analysis is made of the next exemplar of the genre. Eichler’s biographical, historical, and philosophical/spiritual contextualizing of “A Survivor from Warsaw” (1947) seems an unusual choice. But, the fact that this brief monodrama is probably the first major public utterance of the rising awareness of the atrocities described by the narrator and focused attention in a way that only art can. It was also the development of the composer’s revolutionary serially organized music which was, perhaps ironically, very well suited to express the horrors of this age of “great wars”. This section of the book is a masterful integration of political, historical, spiritual elements that provide a compelling mini history, linking individuals and events that shed a fascinating (and devastating) light on this era in musical history. It also places the composer most definitely as a protester, a would be agent of progressive political change. It led this listener to seek to experience more of Schoenberg’s music and was gratified to hear it forever differently and, more so than ever, more essential within western art music. The work was a resounding success at its world premiere in, of all places, New Mexico. The Albuquerque Civic Symphony conducted by Kurt Frederick. 1600 people crowded into the Carlisle Gymnasium on November 4, 1948 were so pleased that the work was repeated, in full, to a deeply moved audience. Hearing this music now, available in many fine interpretations on CD and in video formats, it is all the more stunning that this hardly easy listening tale about horrific events played so well and hit so deeply. And I will never again think of this as one of the composer’s lesser works. Benjamin Britten Moving on to Benjamin Britten and his 1962 “War Requiem”. This music has a prominent place for this writer, having heard a performance by the Chicago Symphony conducted by Mstislav Rostropovich. The cellist, turned conductor was a lifelong progressive political advocate who facilitated a meeting which would become a friendship between Britten and Dmitri Shostakovich among his accomplishments. But, I digress. Eichler’s framing of this composer and music shows a true pacifist composer who encountered the horrors of the First World War as well as subsequent atrocities perhaps one step removed geographically and culturally from the experience of Strauss and Schoenberg. He was a student, then a composer/pianist much admired and supported by the British as he steadily earned his place on the world stage. Early in his rising successes, he managed to insinuate himself to play piano in a series of concerts with Yehudi Menuhin, that toured through war torn Europe to great acclaim. And it is here that the composer encountered first hand, the sights, the stories, the emotions that would forever inform and transform him and his music. This experience is likely one of the seeds that led to the 1962 requiem. Britten utilized the form and Latin texts of the “Missa Pro Defunctis” , the Roman Catholic funeral rites. And he adds a chamber group that plays onstage in front of the full orchestra and chorus (I recall seeing a children’s chorus singing from the topmost seats in Orchestra Hall). The chamber group supports a tenor and a baritone who sing Britten’s settings from the late soldier, then poet/activist Wilfred Owen’s vividly sad and angry poetry. This is a guise not unlike what Leonard Bernstein would do in his anti war “Mass” some 12 years later. Notably, the premiere was to have included tenor Peter Pears (Britten’s life and musical partner), baritone Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, and soprano Galina Vishnevskaya (later the wife of Mstislav Rostropovich). However the Soviet government prevented her from performing this politically hot work. The hope of symbolically including British, German, and Russian artists was to further emphasize the message of the work. Though Vishnevskaya did participate in the glorious 1963 DECCA recording, she was replaced (most successfully) by the fine British soprano Heather Harper for the premiere. Britten himself conducted the chamber group at the premiere with Meredith Davies leading the large orchestra, choir and soloists. The roofless remains of the original Coventry Cathedral In discussing the War Requiem, Eichler recounts his pilgrimage to the site of the newly rebuilt Coventry Cathedral which had been very badly damaged in the war and the work was commissioned to celebrate the consecration of the new edifice which was built next to the 14th century ruins, ruins through which the audience passed following the very successful premiere on July 27th, 1962. Eichler reports that his own experience walking through the ruins was a powerful experience even now, but especially when one knows this history. Dmitri Shostakovich For the book’s finale, Eichler chose a too little known Shostakovich Symphony, his 13th (1962) ( later titled “Babi Yar”). The composer had worked under the repression of the Soviet Empire at least since his opera “Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District” disturbed the Soviet leadership in the 1930s. But he managed to get in a few significant political punches during his long career and continued to produce substantial and fresh new music until his death in 1975. His 5th Symphony won him favor again with the Soviets and the composer’s 7th Symphony “Leningrad”, a paean to the ultimate victory over Nazi forces in 1944 is the stuff of legend, being performed on March 29th of 1942, literally during the siege of Leningrad. Musician soldiers were relieved of their war duties in order to have enough musicians to perform it and strategic bombing raids were done to redirect Nazi bombings and ensure that the music would be heard at its embattled premiere. Eichler’s choice of the 13th Symphony is an apt choice to fit the author’s thesis. The work is a cri de couer, an angry lament raising the awareness of a genocidal slaughter, the evidence of which survived multiple efforts to erase the facts and the evidence from history. It sets the words of the fine Russian poet Yevgeny Yevtushenko (1932-2017) in his poem “Babi Yar” that provided the words. It refers, of course to the genocidal mass murders of Jews, dissidents, and others deemed not worthy of being allowed to live in the Nazi regime at the ravine so named. Accounts vary and much had been done to cover up the murders which numbered up to 30, 000 a day. In fact, there did not exist a memorial for some 100, 000 killed at Babi Yar until 1992. The 13th Symphony premiered on December 18, 1962 in the Great Hall of the Moscow Conservatory. Kiril Kondrashin conducted. Despite controversy and attempts to tamper with the words, pressure to stop the premiere, it was a rousing success. This was only some seven months after the premiere of the Britten War Requiem. Eichler’s account could have ended here but for the fact that, in addition to facilitating a meeting between Britten and Shostakovich, Mistislav Rostropovich smuggled a copy of the 1963 DECCA recording of the War Requiem and a score so that Shostakovich could hear it. And listen he did, with enthusiasm such that Shostakovich was inspired to respond in what would become the composer’s 14th Symphony which was dedicated to Britten. Hence the arts had a conversation about the atrocities of war like never before. The work, incorporating poems by various poets on the subject of death was premiered officially on September 29th, 1969 in Leningrad by the Moscow Chamber Orchestra conducted by Rudolph Barshai. It appears to be inspired in part by the composer’s 1962 orchestration of Modest Mussorgsky’s song cycle, “Songs and Dances of Death” (ca. 1875) and perhaps Gustav Mahler’s “Kindertotenlieder” (1904). The response at the premiere, hardly devoid of criticism, was another resounding success for the aging, ailing composer. The UK premiere was conducted at Aldeburgh by its dedicatee, Benjamin Britten, also to great acclaim. Eichler’s book elegantly describes the genesis of these five works inspired by the history of very real and very shameful atrocities of some 50 years of conflicts which, though they may never be resolved, are truly “Time’s Echo” encased in artistic amber as it were. The memory of this reviewer’s experience of witnessing Maestro Rostrpovich’s reading of Britten’s Requiem so many years later and indeed all subsequent performances of the music chosen here by Eichler hold out a glimmer of hope that these echoes of their time will preserve both the memories of the atrocities themselves as well as the just outrage of the artist’s products in sound for posterity.

items.body: Caught in your head Feel it again What you need now Hope often starts out as a shift in perspective before transforming into something as steady as the stars in the night sky. A person lifts their gaze, allows beauty to feel credible once more, and perceives the future as regaining some of its richness. Music can support this process by creating space for personal experience, presenting an image whose significance shifts depending on who observes it. In this way, light signifies the moment when the world reopens to interpretation, bearing the past while broadening possibilities ahead. That openness runs through “Diamond Rain,” the new single from Los Angeles dark dream-pop duo Magic Wands. Released on August 14th through Metropolis Records, the song finds vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine considering what might appear once a difficult passage in time finally begins to loosen its hold. “The song doesn’t have one fixed meaning. To us, it’s about moving toward the light, finding beauty after darkness and allowing people to discover their own meaning within it.” “Diamond Rain” glows with starfire, carried by a deep, chorus-laden bassline with the imposing scale of 4AD’s post-punk catalog. A crisp drum-machine snare gives the song its dance-floor pull, while sustained guitar hangs overhead in sheets of cold light, breaking into bright points around Dexy’s gauzed lead vocal. The arrangement is dense without becoming airless, and each return to the title phrase seems to lift the music another degree. It ranks among Magic Wands’ most immediate and accomplished songs; six albums into their career, the Valentines plainly still have more than a few tricks up their sleeves. The lyrics start within the mind, where emotions cycle and longing is hard to specify, then shift outward with images of the sun, pale water, lost letters, and departure. “Save it all, for the diamond rain,” Dexy sings. The title presents a compelling contradiction by linking the fury of a storm with the beauty and refraction of a jewel. Its rain can harm, cleanse, hide, or shine light, and the recurring refrain offers a surface for listeners to project their own memories. Magic Wands make that ambiguity visible in the accompanying homemade video “using old cameras, lights and mirrors to create textures and effects that give it a dreamlike feeling.” Extreme close-ups of eyes and mouths overlap with guitars, hands, and ghosted profiles; monochrome images suddenly bloom into acid green, electric blue, and molten red. Bright flecks scatter across the frame like snow caught in headlights as mirrored exposures divide faces into doubles. Elsewhere, horizontal interference and bold blocks of lyric text fill the screen, becoming part of the moving collage. The practical imperfections give the clip its tactile charge, as though vision were returning in fragments of glare, color, and reflection. Watch the video for “Diamond Rain” below: Magic Wands formed in Nashville in 2008 after Chris Valentine discovered Dexy’s song “Teenage Love” online. While they were still living on opposite sides of the country, Chris sent Dexy an actual magic wand through the mail; the gift eventually gave the duo their name. Dexy relocated from Los Angeles to Nashville, and their exchange of songs developed into the Magic Love & Dreams EP in 2009. The xx subsequently remixed their track “Warrior,” while the 2012 debut album Aloha Moon brought the pair to a wider audience and preceded a tour supporting The Jesus and Mary Chain. After settling in Los Angeles, Magic Wands continued with Jupiter (2016), Abrakadabra (2018), Illuminate (2020), Switch (2023), and Cascades (2025). Across those records, Dexy and Chris have shifted between live rhythm sections, drum machines, distorted guitars, and droning synthesizers while retaining the intimate vocal interplay at the center of the band. Their 2026 output has already included the Wishing Well and Remixes EPs, along with their reworking of Peter Murphy’s “Swoon.” “Diamond Rain” now opens the way to a still-untitled Magic Wands album expected in early 2027. “Diamond Rain” is out now via Metropolis Records. Listen to the single on streaming platforms here, and order it here. items.body: Desde cuando te pregunto si tuyo puedo ser? Hace tiempo que no siento fallo por no perder No lamento lo que no pude tener Solo arrepiento mirarte y saber Five albums into Casual Confrontation, Frankie Diez has decided that refinement is overrated when you can instead build a nightclub out of sheet metal, subwoofers, bad memories, and one unwelcome face in the crowd. ARREBATO, the first single from the forthcoming BASTION, takes reggaeton’s dembow gait and marches it straight into industrial machinery, where darkwave synths hover overhead, and the breakdowns come down with Ministry-sized force. The title means “rapture,” and Diez draws part of its charge from Iván Zulueta’s 1979 Spanish arthouse horror film Arrebato, a movie where obsession becomes appetite and starts swallowing people. This song is about the moment attention curdles into surveillance. Somebody from years ago keeps turning up where the singer goes, particularly in the dark club where being found feels less romantic than invasive. Desire has crossed a line, and Diez answers with disgust sharp enough to leave teeth marks. The bilingual chorus gives the confrontation force because the switch into English lands with the plainness of somebody abandoning diplomacy. There is no ornate misery here, no candlewax poetry about doomed lovers circling each other forever. The emotional center is recognition: realizing that another person has interpreted access as entitlement, then saying the ugly necessary words aloud. Musically, Diez has identified a seemingly obvious combination that, in hindsight, raises the question of why more artists haven’t explored it. Reggaeton already employs repetition as a form of physical persuasion, while EBM and industrial music have long integrated themes of menace, machinery, and bodily discipline. By layering the dembow rhythm, typical of Bad Bunny, beneath synth textures reminiscent of Ultra Sunn, and allowing the track to develop a metallic impact similar to what Ministry once emphasized as a civic duty, “Reggaeton Gótico” transitions from seeming like a joke made at closing time to presenting a viable, compelling concept. Diez explains the connection through experience rather than genre theory: “I always listened to reggaeton growing up in both Puerto Rico and in Miami, and the genre fusion always felt natural, since much of reggaeton can easily have somewhat of a dark-clubbing atmosphere already.” That background keeps ARREBATO from feeling like two record collections stapled together. The rhythm sits inside the song’s bloodstream, while the harsher electronic elements intensify its sense of danger. By the breakdown, the club has become a pressure chamber and the confrontation feels public, which may be the point: stalkers thrive on ambiguity, private fear, and the hope that their target will remain polite. Watch the lyric video below: ARREBATO ends that politeness. If BASTION follows this path, Casual Confrontation may have stumbled onto a nasty little hybrid with real legs: music for dancing, recoiling, and finally telling somebody who will not take the hint exactly where the door is. Listen to ARREBATO below and order the single here. items.body: Rue Oberkampf release “Wehmut” in mid-October 2026 on Young And Cold Records, their third full album for the Augsburg label and their first since “Liebe” in 2022. The record runs six tracks: “Tonight”, “Come on Moon”, “Blanc Poney”, “Into the Woid”, “Sonne” and “Darkness”. Bandcamp gives the release date as 15 October; the label’s own shop and its distributor both say 16 October. Wehmut by Rue Oberkampf The Munich duo take the title from a German word with no direct English equivalent, and open their own note on the record by saying so. “It describes a feeling suspended between melancholy and nostalgia. A longing for something lost or remembered. A yearning for a beautiful place you once knew, or one you have never been to, yet somehow miss all the same.” They credit the album to walking the Goldsteig trail in the Bavarian Forest, to a sea crossing between Antwerp and Hanko in Finland, to the “Wanderweg” zines put out by Haus Nostromo, and to a mixture of Zeitgeist and post-metal, closing with an invitation to “be wehmütig with us”. Formats and credits for Rue Oberkampf’s ‘Wehmut’ The vinyl edition is a gatefold sleeve with a lyrics inlay, pressed for the first run on brown transparent vinyl. The CD comes in a digipak with an eight-page lyrics booklet, and a digital edition runs alongside both. Pre-orders are open through Bandcamp and the Young And Cold shop. Julia de Jouy and Oliver Maier wrote the music and lyrics. Johannes Vopel mixed “Tonight”, “Come on Moon”, “Into the Woid” and “Sonne”; Wolfgang Lehmann mixed “Blanc Poney” and “Darkness”. Ludwig Maier mastered the digital and CD editions and Eric Van Wonterghem mastered the vinyl. Josip Tijan of Thymian plays acoustic guitar on “Darkness”. The field recordings are placed as precisely as the studio credits: forest sound for “Darkness” captured at the Buchberger Leite gorge near Freyung, waves for “Sonne” recorded at Falkensteiner Strand in Kiel, and Scottish owls on “Into the Woid” taken from the BBC Sound Library. Kinnat Sóley designed the artwork, which is built on a Vorarlberg Landesbibliothek photograph titled “Nadelbäume im Nebel”. The announcement follows “The Singles 2018-2026”, the eight-track compilation released on 9 July 2026 that collected “Eternity”, “Eiszeit”, “Solitude”, “I Won’t Surrender (Brutal Edit)”, “Negativraum”, “Sans Toi”, “Deine Augen” and “Never Stop to Dance” on vinyl and CD, both hand-numbered and limited to 666 copies with no repress. About Rue Oberkampf Julia de Jouy, Oliver Maier and Damien De-Vir formed Rue Oberkampf in 2016, all three having DJed in southern Germany before that. The name is taken from the Paris street and metro station named after Christophe-Philippe Oberkampf, and de Jouy’s own pseudonym points at the same figure through the toile de Jouy fabric his factory produced. They sing in French, German and English, and set 1980s electronic darkwave against a techno pulse. The first single, “Le Train”, was a cover of Absolute Body Control‘s “Melting Away” that Dirk Ivens passed on to his own audience. The “Waveclash” EP came out on No Emb Blanc in 2018, and the “Sans Toi” lathe-cut split with Sunday Victim on Circonstances Aggravantes in 2019. The debut album “Christophe-Philippe” landed on Young And Cold Records at the end of 2019 and has been repressed twice since. “Negativraum” appeared on Ant-Zen in 2020, and the second album “Liebe” on Young And Cold in 2022. The mini-album “Essenz” followed on 30 October 2024 and was repressed in 2025. In a 2020 Side-Line interview the band described a recording method split across a home studio in Passau, a small room in Munich and the Young And Cold studio in Augsburg. De-Vir left in 2023, and the writing credits since carry only de Jouy and Maier. Young And Cold Records was founded in Augsburg on 1 May 2012 by Marcel Leidenroth and Daniel Hallhuber, who run it with Micha Oswald. It began with hand-dubbed cassettes and now lists more than two hundred releases across post-punk, wave and underground electronics, with Twin Tribes among its widest-selling acts. “Wehmut” is the fourth Rue Oberkampf record it has issued, and arrives four years after “Liebe”.

items.body: Ironic Sweden, the Swedish synthpop and darkwave duo built around producer Dan Ritzen, release “Walk With Angels” on 21 August 2026 through the Danish label Town And Towers Records. The single comes with two remixes and an official video, which premieres on the label’s YouTube channel at midnight Swedish time the same day. It is a song about dying, written in the first person, and Ritzen says he wrote it as an account of how he expects to meet that moment. Ritzen puts the subject plainly rather than at a distance: “A song from the heart. About a subject we rarely talk about. Our own death. I wanted to create a song, where I could explain how I think, I will react on that day. When it’s time for me to go. And tell the people that I’ve done all I wanted to do in my life, so now I can go in peace.” Inside the lyrics of ‘Walk With Angels’ The track sets a hypnotic electronic pulse under melancholic melodies, and the words work through a set of borrowed death images: a dealer handing over a dead man’s hand, coins put aside for the ferryman, a compass needle that no longer points north. The chorus – “Walk with angels / They’ll guide me tonight / I’m leaving earth now without a strife” – reads as acceptance rather than protest. The angels themselves turn out to be less consoling than the chorus suggests. In the final verse they arrive with broken wings and flaming swords, crying, pointing at the narrator. The single is a pre-save at the moment and lands on Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, Amazon Music, SoundCloud and Tidal on the 21st. It is not on Bandcamp, where Ironic Sweden hosts the rest of its catalogue. The two remixes have been serviced to radio, but neither the remixers nor a separate remix release has been announced. About Ironic Sweden Dan Ritzen started making electronic music in Sweden in the late 1990s as Obscene Inside, working with Fredrik Hansson on an Atari 1040ST and a Yamaha CS1X until Hansson left after about a year. The project became Ironic in the mid-2000s and put out a self-titled EP in a very small run, then took its current name in 2010. The debut EP “Player” followed in December 2017 in an edition of a hundred CDs and records, and remixes of it appeared the following April. Singles and EPs came steadily from there: “King” in October 2018, “Dansmusik” in May 2019, “Pictures” that November, “Dina drömmar” in October 2020, “Universe Friend” in April 2021 and “When I Cry” that October, then the album “Icu” in October 2022. In mid-2023 Ritzen expanded the act into a trio with vocalist Stefan Kauppila Johansson and singer Tezz Markström, and the album “Evolution” arrived on 11 November 2023. Ironic Sweden signed to Town And Towers Records in December 2023, and Side-Line covered the first release under that deal, the double single “Lost Eden” and “Media Whore”, on 22 March 2024. Both sides were produced by Callum Melville, who works as Calibeats; he and his brother Luke later remixed “Media Whore” for a March 2025 release. Markström left in April 2025, and the act has run as a duo since, drawing in guest vocalists on individual tracks – Camila on “My Ego” and Monica on “The Light”, both released on 7 November 2025. “A Night In July” closed 2025 and “Get It Right” followed in February 2026. The band is based in Småland in south-east Sweden and records in a caravan using Logic Pro X, with a sound palette that runs from synthesisers and drum pads through to scrap metal and animal bones. Town And Towers Records, run by Stig Wintendorff out of Gentofte in Denmark, is a member of the Danish independent labels association DUP and works across darkwave, synthpop, italo disco and electropop; Oui Plastique is next on its release schedule, on 4 September. “Walk With Angels” is the first Ironic Sweden single since “Get It Right” in February 2026.

items.body: Sina Matix, the Jacksonville dark electro project, released “Killing The Curse” on 7 August 2026 as a standalone digital single. The 4:07 track pushes harder and faster than the surrounding catalogue, setting an angrier vocal against an upbeat EBM pulse. An official video went up on the artist’s own YouTube channel a day earlier, on 6 August. KILLING THE CURSE by SINA MATIX The song is about a stretch of life that does not end on its own. Sina Matix sums it up on the Bandcamp page as “living in toxicity for 5 years and coming to terms that it’s time to reboot your life”, and the press release expands on the same idea: bad luck, divorce, backstabbing and a fear of commitment running for years, until the person finds the strength to press reboot. Where ‘Killing The Curse’ sits in the Sina Matix run of releases The single is self-released and carries no label. It is available as a digital track on Bandcamp in 24-bit/48 kHz, and on Spotify and the other main streaming services. Moon Coil Media handled the announcement. “Killing The Curse” is the fourth Sina Matix release of 2026 and does not belong to “A Dark Place”, the six-track EP issued on 1 May. That run began with the album “Goths Stuck In Airports” on 9 January, followed by the single “This Is Not AI” on 6 March. Two collaborations bookended the turn of the year: “Evil Deals” with Normoria on 2 January and “Crucified” with Matias Nix in December 2025. About Sina Matix Sina Matix is a solo project based in Jacksonville, Florida. The musician behind it does not publish a legal name and works through a chain of aliases: recording as OR from 1995 to 2008, DJing as DJ Question? between 1999 and 2011, then moving into visual work from 2011 as VJ R-M8E and Cinematic Manipulation. The Sina Matix name dates from 2022. Asked directly in a March 2025 interview whether anyone else was involved, the artist answered: “I’m the only one at this point that is part of SINA MATIX.” Side-Line’s earlier coverage notes an origin in Houston, Texas, before the move to Florida. The project’s own label for its music is “dark dramatic electro”, a term it applies to cinematic arrangements built around sampled dialogue and dark subject matter; pushed on genre, the artist points to EBM, darkwave, goth, industrial and film scores, and names Fad Gadget’s “GAG”, Nine Inch Nails’ “The Downward Spiral” and Pink Floyd’s “The Wall” as formative records. The Bandcamp tags on the new single read across the same span, from dark electro and EBM through to industrial techno. The first tracks appeared in 2022 with “Worthless”, followed by “The System” in July 2024 and “Burn” and “Monsters” that September. The debut EP “Cursed” arrived on 31 January 2025 with six tracks on isolation and worthlessness, and Side-Line covered it that February. A signed CD edition limited to fifty numbered copies, “Blessed”, followed on 11 April 2025 with remixes by Assemblage 23, Matt Hart, Ex-VoTo, Stoneburner and Aktivity 512, and the remix album “Burn: The Inferno Mixes” had come out two weeks before that. Singles ran through the rest of 2025: “Flesh and Machine” in September, “Kanokwan” in December and the two collaborations that closed the year. “Killing The Curse” is the sixteenth Sina Matix release on Bandcamp in four years, and the first since “A Dark Place” in May.
